title: Why do we sleep?
subtitle: Body & brain
subject: sciences
description: We spend a third of our lives asleep. It is not wasted time: sleep cleans the brain, repairs the body and etches memories into place.

hero.hook: Sleeping is not switching off: it is the body's great night shift.

blocks.text: Over a 75-year life, we sleep for nearly **25 years**. For a long time sleep was thought to be no more than a pause. In fact it is active work, as vital as drinking or eating.
Science still does not have every answer about “why” we sleep. But it knows very well what happens when we do not, and what the night quietly repairs.
In **1964**, the American student **Randy Gardner** went **11 days** without sleep. Hallucinations, paranoia, a mind coming apart: proof that the brain cannot hold up without rest.

blocks.caption: Sleep, essential to the recovery of both brain and body

blocks.text: In rats, total sleep deprivation kills in **2 to 3 weeks**, like starvation. In humans, a rare genetic illness, **fatal familial insomnia**, also ends in death. In everyday terms, 17 hours awake is the equivalent of a blood alcohol level of **0.5 g/l**. The brain then forces [[microsleeps]], short involuntary breaks in consciousness.
After his record, Randy Gardner slept **14 hours** straight. He woke up able to function, but his sleep took weeks to find a normal rhythm again.

sections.title: At night, the brain cleans house

blocks.text: During sleep the brain does not stop, it switches mode. The **hippocampus**, a seahorse-shaped structure central to memory, “replays” the day and sends the information on to the [[Neocortex]], the outer layer of the brain, for lasting storage. The result: we often learn **20 to 40%** better after a good night.

Deep sleep also releases **growth hormone**, which repairs muscle and tissue, and boosts [[cytokines]], the signaling molecules of the immune system. Another major discovery: the [[glymphatic system]], a brain drainage network **ten times** more active at night. It flushes out waste, including the proteins linked to Alzheimer's risk.
During deep sleep, brain cells shrink by about **60%**. The space that opens up lets the cleaning fluid circulate much more freely.

sections.title: Who sleeps how much, and how

blocks.text: Cats sleep **12 to 16 hours**: predators in safety. Giraffes sometimes make do with **30 minutes to 2 hours**, taken in short naps, ready to run. Dolphins sleep with **one hemisphere**, half the brain, at a time, so they can keep surfacing to breathe.

Babies sleep up to **18 hours**, with a great deal of [[REM sleep]], the dreaming phase with its rapid eye movements. That phase supports [[synaptogenesis]], the building of connections between neurons.

sections.title: The internal clock and blue light

blocks.text: Two forces push us toward bed: the tiredness that builds up during the day, and [[Circadian rhythms and melatonin]], the internal clock set to **24 hours**. When the light fades, the brain releases **melatonin**, a hormone that prepares the body for sleep without forcing it.

Screens in the evening fool that clock and delay falling asleep. You cannot really “catch up” on a sleep debt at the weekend: the tiredness drops, but not all the damage. Regular hours and a dark, cool room remain your best allies.
Sleep cleans the brain, repairs the body and consolidates memory. Total deprivation kills within weeks: sleeping is not a luxury, it is vital maintenance.
